column1:
Cautiously positive macro tone with a dovish tilt remains appropriate given strong labor conditions and inflation near 2 percent, but the SLOOS points to tightening credit supply and softer demand around late-2018/early-2019 that reinforces patience and downside risk monitoring.

Key SLOOS takeaways that temper the tone:
- Business credit: Banks tightened standards on C&I loans and construction/land development, widened loan rate spreads, and tightened other terms; they expected tighter standards for C&I and CRE and weaker business loan demand in 2019.
- Residential real estate: Reported weaker demand for mortgages and HELOCs; standards were unchanged for GSE-eligible mortgages and HELOCs, but banks expected tighter standards for nonconforming jumbos; weaker demand was also reported for construction and land development loans.
- Consumer credit: Standards were unchanged for some categories (e.g., auto), but banks reported tighter standards in parts of consumer lending and wider spreads; demand was generally unchanged to weaker; banks expected deterioration in performance for mortgages and for nonprime consumer loans.
- Rationale: Collateral values and risk concerns were cited as reasons for tightening.

Implication: These SLOOS signals, alongside the FSR’s volatility, wider spreads, and elevated corporate leverage, validate the FOMC’s “patient” stance and modestly offset the otherwise solid macro backdrop. Net assessment nudges closer to neutral from mildly positive.
